values.stages.3: Recovery, Measurement, and an Integrated Project
values.goal: Understand WebGPU devices, resources, and the command model, and validate rendering and compute through correctness and overall cost.
values.capstone: A small particle experiment with support guidance, device loss recovery, compute updates, and readback validation

values.title: Adapter·Device·Pipeline
values.concepts.0.title: Support Requirements
values.concepts.0.explanation: WebGPU requires both a secure context and browser and device support. Even when navigator.gpu exists, the adapter request can return null.
values.concepts.1.title: Initialization
values.concepts.1.explanation: Obtain a device from the adapter, then create resources and pipelines with that device. Handle initialization failure as an on-screen state before starting the render loop.
values.outcomes.1: Handle initialization failure as a recoverable state.
values.steps.0: In main.js, check isSecureContext and navigator.gpu and display the status.
values.steps.1: Call requestAdapter and requestDevice in order and record the reason for failure.
values.steps.2: Separate normal, missing-API, and adapter-null cases into injectable functions and check each screen output.
values.variables.0.name: Adapter response
values.variables.0.expected: An unsupported-environment message is expected instead of an exception or blank screen.
values.criteria.0: Display a status string in all three initialization branches.
values.criteria.1: Create device resources only after success.
values.questions.0: Which failures does checking API presence alone miss?
values.questions.1: How do a secure context and device support differ?
values.prerequisites: TypedArray, asynchronous JavaScript, and the WebGL pipeline
values.environment: The existing webgpu-01 preview is a starting point. It does not replace implementation or validation of the entire subsequent assignment. values.title: Negotiating Features and limits
values.concepts.0.title: Optional Features
values.concepts.0.explanation: Not every adapter provides the same optional features. Check the supported list before requesting a feature you need.
values.concepts.1.title: Limits
values.concepts.1.explanation: Resource sizes and binding counts have device limits. Restrict inputs according to device.limits instead of guessing large values.
values.outcomes.1: Write input checks based on limits.
values.steps.0: In capabilities.js, display only the required adapter.features and limits entries in a table.
values.steps.1: Write a requestDevice descriptor that distinguishes required and optional features.
values.steps.2: Disable unsupported optional features and validate the maximum buffer-size input.
values.variables.0.name: Optional feature
values.variables.0.expected: The feature is expected to be enabled only on supported devices, with the default path retained elsewhere.
values.criteria.0: State required and optional features separately.
values.criteria.1: Reject inputs exceeding limits before creating resources.
values.questions.0: Why distinguish adapter limits from requested device limits?
values.questions.1: Must an optional-feature failure shut down the entire app?
values.prerequisites: Continue using the output and notes from unit 1. Preserve the previous inputs and reference outputs before the Negotiating Features and limits experiment.

values.title: Canvas Configuration and the Current Texture
values.concepts.0.title: Display Target
values.concepts.0.explanation: The canvas context connects the device to the display format. Obtain the current frame texture each frame and use it as a render attachment.
values.concepts.1.title: Matching Formats
values.concepts.1.explanation: The pipeline color target format must match the attachment format. Query the browser's preferred format through the API.
values.outcomes.0: Connect the canvas to GPU output.
values.steps.0: In canvas.js, call getContext('webgpu') and getPreferredCanvasFormat.
values.steps.1: After configure, create a clear pass with getCurrentTexture().createView().
values.steps.2: Change the background color, obtain a new view each frame, and record the configure values.
values.variables.0.name: Clear color
values.variables.0.expected: The entire attachment color is expected to change even without geometry.
values.criteria.0: Obtain the current texture view for each frame.
values.criteria.1: Record the preferred format and pipeline target format as the same value.
values.questions.0: Why is retaining a previous frame's texture a problem?
values.questions.1: How does a CSS background color differ from an attachment clear?
values.prerequisites: Continue using the output and notes from unit 2. Preserve the previous inputs and reference outputs before the Canvas Configuration and the Current Texture experiment.

values.title: Recording and Submitting Commands
values.concepts.0.title: Recording Stage
values.concepts.0.explanation: A command encoder does not complete work immediately. End the pass, create a command buffer, and submit it to the queue.
values.concepts.1.title: Completion
values.concepts.1.explanation: Returning from submit does not mean GPU work has finished. Wait for completion only at observation points that require it.
values.steps.0: In commands.js, write the createCommandEncoder·beginRenderPass·end·finish·submit sequence.
values.steps.1: Record two clear colors in separate submissions and check the last color on screen.
values.steps.2: Log the times before and after submit and when onSubmittedWorkDone completes.
values.variables.0.name: Submission count
values.variables.0.expected: The last clear result is expected to be visible, with separate submission and completion logs.
values.criteria.0: Every pass reaches finish after end.
values.criteria.1: Record submission and completion as separate items.
values.questions.0: Is command-recording time GPU execution time?
values.questions.1: What parallelism is reduced by waiting for completion every frame?
values.prerequisites: Continue using the output and notes from unit 3. Preserve the previous inputs and reference outputs before the Recording and Submitting Commands experiment.

values.title: Shader Modules and Diagnostics
values.concepts.0.title: Module Diagnostics
values.concepts.0.explanation: WGSL syntax and type errors can be checked through the shader module's compilation info. Connect error line positions to the source.
values.concepts.1.title: Pipeline Validation
values.concepts.1.explanation: Even a valid module can fail pipeline creation when its entry point or target contract does not match. Record compilation and pipeline validation separately.
values.outcomes.1: Distinguish module errors from pipeline errors.
values.steps.0: Write minimal vertex and fragment functions in shader.wgsl.
values.steps.1: Use getCompilationInfo to display messages and lineNum in the UI.
values.steps.2: Introduce a typo and an incorrect entryPoint separately, then restore the code and display a triangle.
values.variables.0.name: Entry point
values.variables.0.expected: The pipeline stage is expected to fail even if the module passes syntax checks.
values.criteria.0: Record syntax errors and entry point errors separately.
values.criteria.1: The triangle reappears after restoring the original source.
values.questions.0: Why can a pipeline fail when the module has no errors?
values.questions.1: How can asynchronous diagnostics be prevented from overwriting new-code messages with old ones?
values.prerequisites: Continue using the output and notes from unit 4. Preserve the previous inputs and reference outputs before the Shader Modules and Diagnostics experiment.

values.title: Vertex Buffers and Attributes
values.concepts.0.title: Byte Contract
values.concepts.0.explanation: A vertex buffer layout declares the stride and each attribute's offset and format. Confusing TypedArray element indices with byte offsets reads incorrect values.
values.concepts.1.title: Upload
values.concepts.1.explanation: GPUBufferUsage specifies which commands may use a buffer. A queue.writeBuffer destination must include COPY_DST usage.
values.outcomes.1: Connect a CPU array to GPU vertex input.
values.steps.0: In vertices.js, create three vertices with two position components and three color components.
values.steps.1: Declare a 20-byte stride and offsets of 0·8 bytes in the pipeline.
values.steps.2: Upload to a VERTEX|COPY_DST buffer and inspect each vertex color on screen.
values.variables.0.name: arrayStride
values.variables.0.expected: The same triangle is expected when the data and layout are changed together.
values.criteria.0: Write a byte-offset table for the three vertices.
values.criteria.1: Vertex positions and colors match across both layouts.
values.questions.0: How are format and the TypedArray type related?
values.questions.1: What happens if only the stride changes while the data stays unchanged?
values.prerequisites: Continue using the output and notes from unit 5. Preserve the previous inputs and reference outputs before the Vertex Buffers and Attributes experiment.

values.title: Indices and Primitives
values.concepts.0.title: Reuse
values.concepts.0.explanation: An index buffer reuses the same vertex data across multiple triangles. Index values must fall within the actual vertex count.
values.concepts.1.title: Primitive Interpretation
values.concepts.1.explanation: Primitive topology and front face settings affect vertex connectivity and front-face classification. The same data can produce different results with different settings.
values.steps.0: In quad.js, write four vertices and six Uint16Array indices.
values.steps.1: Connect an INDEX|COPY_DST buffer with setIndexBuffer('uint16') and call drawIndexed.
values.steps.2: Reverse one triangle's index order, change cullMode, and compare the results.
values.variables.0.name: cullMode
values.variables.0.expected: Only the triangle with reversed winding is expected to disappear.
values.criteria.0: Draw a rectangle with four vertices and six indices.
values.criteria.1: Record both winding cases and the culling results.
values.questions.0: What goes wrong when the index format does not match the array's byte count?
values.questions.1: Which coordinate transforms affect the front face on screen?
values.prerequisites: Continue using the output and notes from unit 6. Preserve the previous inputs and reference outputs before the Indices and Primitives experiment.

values.title: Uniforms and Bind Groups
values.concepts.0.title: Binding Contract
values.concepts.0.explanation: A bind group connects resources to the shader's group and binding locations. Resource types and shader visibility are also part of the layout.
values.concepts.1.title: Small Updates
values.concepts.1.explanation: Uniforms suit small inputs shared by many invocations. Buffer values can be updated without creating a pipeline each time.
values.outcomes.1: Update small inputs without recreating resources.
values.steps.0: In uniform.wgsl, declare a vec4f color uniform at binding 0.
values.steps.1: In uniforms.js, create a 16-byte UNIFORM|COPY_DST buffer and a bind group.
values.steps.2: Connect color sliders to queue.writeBuffer and record the number of pipelines created.
values.variables.0.name: Color input
values.variables.0.expected: Only the triangle color is expected to change, without recreating the pipeline.
values.criteria.0: Both color inputs are reflected correctly.
values.criteria.1: Changing the color ten times does not increase the pipeline creation count.
values.questions.0: Is a binding number an offset inside a buffer?
values.questions.1: Can a uniform buffer be used in place of a vertex buffer?
values.prerequisites: Continue using the output and notes from unit 7. Preserve the previous inputs and reference outputs before the Uniforms and Bind Groups experiment.

values.title: Uniform Struct Alignment
values.concepts.0.title: Internal Layout
values.concepts.0.explanation: WGSL struct member alignment and size determine the CPU byte layout. A vec3f alignment of 16 and size of 12 are different concepts.
values.concepts.1.title: Binding Offset
values.concepts.1.explanation: Struct member alignment and dynamic uniform offset limits are separate rules. Dynamic offsets must follow the device's minimum alignment.
values.steps.0: In layout.md, calculate offsets 0·12 and size 16 for a struct containing color:vec3f, gain:f32.
values.steps.1: Write color and gain separately with DataView and check the output color.
values.steps.2: When creating two struct slots, round the slot stride up using minUniformBufferOffsetAlignment.
values.variables.0.name: gain offset
values.variables.0.expected: The gain read by the shader is expected to remain unchanged, exposing the layout error.
values.criteria.0: Provide a table of member offsets, sizes, and alignments.
values.criteria.1: With the correct layout, the two slots' colors and gain values do not mix.
values.questions.0: Does placing f32 after vec3 always require 4 bytes of padding?
values.questions.1: Can dynamic offset alignment be treated as equal to struct size?
values.prerequisites: Continue using the output and notes from unit 8. Preserve the previous inputs and reference outputs before the Uniform Struct Alignment experiment.

values.title: Matrices and Cameras
values.concepts.0.title: Transform Order
values.concepts.0.explanation: The multiplication order of world, view, and projection matrices determines how positions are interpreted. Reordering the same matrices changes translation and the center of rotation.
values.concepts.1.title: Depth Range
values.concepts.1.explanation: WebGPU's clip depth range differs from WebGL's. Check that the projection function follows the target API's depth convention.
values.steps.0: Separate model, view, and projection matrices in camera.js.
values.steps.1: Upload a 64-byte mat4x4f uniform and return the multiplied position from the vertex shader.
values.steps.2: Print clip z/w for markers on the near and far planes and check the 0..1 range.
values.variables.0.name: Matrix order
values.variables.0.baseline: Product intended to produce translation followed by rotation
values.variables.0.expected: The object center and orbital motion are expected to change.
values.criteria.0: Record normalized depths for near-plane and far-plane markers.
values.criteria.1: Compare the center positions of both matrix orders numerically.
values.questions.0: Which range changes if you use a WebGL projection matrix unchanged?
values.questions.1: How do you match CPU matrix storage order to shader operations?
values.prerequisites: Continue using the output and notes from unit 9. Preserve the previous inputs and reference outputs before the Matrices and Cameras experiment.

values.title: Textures and Samplers
values.concepts.0.title: Separate Roles
values.concepts.0.explanation: A texture stores texel data, while a sampler determines interpolation and boundary handling. Connect them through separate bindings.
values.concepts.1.title: Input Color
values.concepts.1.explanation: The image color representation and texture format affect the displayed result. First check orientation and channels with a small pattern you create yourself.
values.outcomes.1: Compare the effects of sampler settings.
values.steps.0: In texture.js, create a 2×2 RGBA pattern and upload it with queue.writeTexture.
values.steps.1: Connect texture_2d and sampler bindings to the fragment shader.
values.steps.2: Compare UV orientation and nearest and linear sampling, and record the four corner colors.
values.variables.0.name: filter
values.variables.0.expected: Colors are expected to blend smoothly at boundaries.
values.criteria.0: Check the positions of all four corner colors in the 2×2 pattern.
values.criteria.1: Save the difference in boundary output between the two filters.
values.questions.0: Why treat a texture and sampler as separate resources?
values.questions.1: How do you distinguish a UV Y-direction error from an image row-order error?
values.prerequisites: Continue using the output and notes from unit 10. Preserve the previous inputs and reference outputs before the Textures and Samplers experiment.

values.title: Depth Attachments
values.concepts.0.title: Depth Testing
values.concepts.0.explanation: A depth texture stores the front-to-back relationship of fragments. A color attachment alone cannot provide occlusion independent of drawing order.
values.concepts.1.title: Lifetime
values.concepts.1.explanation: When the size changes, recreate the depth texture at the same size. Release the replaced texture when it is no longer used.
values.steps.0: Add a depth24plus texture and depthStencil settings in depth.js.
values.steps.1: Place two overlapping triangles at different depths and reverse their draw order.
values.steps.2: Record depthClearValue, depthCompare, and depthWriteEnabled while comparing results.
values.variables.0.name: Depth testing
values.variables.0.expected: Opaque-shape occlusion is expected to be independent of draw order.
values.criteria.0: The same shape is in front in both draw orders.
values.criteria.1: The depth attachment size matches the color output size.
values.questions.0: Is the same depth-write policy suitable for transparent objects?
values.questions.1: Why must the depth clear value and comparison be chosen together?
values.prerequisites: Continue using the output and notes from unit 11. Preserve the previous inputs and reference outputs before the Depth Attachments experiment.

values.title: Resize and Sample Count
values.concepts.0.title: Actual Resolution
values.concepts.0.explanation: CSS size and drawing buffer size may differ. Account for DPR while keeping within the device's texture-size limits.
values.concepts.1.title: MSAA
values.concepts.1.explanation: A multisample attachment can pass its display result to a resolve target. The pipeline and attachment sampleCount must match.
values.steps.0: In resize.js, read sizes with ResizeObserver and determine buffer dimensions using DPR and limits.
values.steps.1: Create color and depth textures with sampleCount 4 and use the current canvas view as resolveTarget.
values.steps.2: Replace attachments on resize and save edge images for sampleCount 1 and 4.
values.variables.0.name: sampleCount
values.variables.0.expected: Triangle-edge stair stepping is expected to decrease while attachment cost increases.
values.criteria.0: Attachment dimensions match at three canvas sizes.
values.criteria.1: Compare edge images for 1·4 samples at the same point in time.
values.questions.0: Does MSAA solve all shader aliasing?
values.questions.1: How should texture creation be handled when the window size becomes 0?
values.prerequisites: Continue using the output and notes from unit 12. Preserve the previous inputs and reference outputs before the Resize and Sample Count experiment.

values.title: Buffers and Render Passes
values.concepts.0.title: Integrated Path
values.concepts.0.explanation: CPU arrays become shader inputs through buffers and bindings. A render pass combines output attachments with pipeline and draw state.
values.concepts.1.title: Error Scope
values.concepts.1.explanation: Place an error scope around operations that may fail validation. Record descriptors and messages together rather than hiding errors.
values.outcomes.1: Diagnose and recover from validation failures.
values.steps.0: In renderer.js, combine vertex, color-uniform, attachment, and draw paths into one function.
values.steps.1: After pushErrorScope('validation'), create a minimal case using a buffer with incorrect usage and display the popErrorScope result.
values.steps.2: Restore the usage, change color and resolution inputs, and rerun the same rendering path.
values.variables.0.name: buffer usage
values.variables.0.expected: Uniform-binding validation is expected to fail, with color updates resuming after recovery.
values.criteria.0: Explain the five links from the CPU color value to screen output.
values.criteria.1: Record the intentional validation error and recover normal rendering.
values.questions.0: Where do pass settings and pipeline settings meet?
values.questions.1: Does a successful submit alone guarantee rendering correctness?
values.prerequisites: Continue using the output and notes from unit 13. Preserve the previous inputs and reference outputs before the Buffers and Render Passes experiment.

values.title: A First Compute Array Transform
values.concepts.0.title: Parallel Indices
values.concepts.0.explanation: global_invocation_id can identify the element to process. Dispatch size depends on both element count and workgroup size.
values.concepts.1.title: Bounds Checks
values.concepts.1.explanation: The final workgroup may contain more invocations than actual data elements. In independent-element kernels, check the length before accessing data.
values.steps.0: In compute.wgsl, write a kernel that doubles each input array element.
values.steps.1: Create two storage buffers and a compute pipeline, and dispatch ceil(N/64) workgroups.
values.steps.2: Use N=65 and copy the output to a staging buffer to check through the last element.
values.variables.0.name: Array length
values.variables.0.expected: Only one element in the second workgroup is expected to perform a valid calculation.
values.criteria.0: All 65 results match the CPU doubling results.
values.criteria.1: Exclude invocations beyond the length before buffer access.
values.questions.0: Does dispatchWorkgroups take an element count?
values.questions.1: Does adding a barrier require reviewing early-return conditions?

values.title: Storage and Ping-Pong
values.concepts.0.title: Write Conflicts
values.concepts.0.explanation: Reading neighboring values while updating the same array can make results depend on execution order. Separate input and output ping-pong buffers preserve the previous state.
values.concepts.1.title: Swapping Steps
values.concepts.1.explanation: After one step, swap the read and write roles for the next. Two bind groups can be created beforehand and alternated.
values.outcomes.1: Manage data dependencies in repeated computation.
values.steps.0: In simulation.wgsl, write a kernel that outputs the average of three neighboring values.
values.steps.1: Create A→B and B→A bind groups and alternate them each step.
values.steps.2: Compare three steps with CPU calculations using separate input and output arrays.
values.variables.0.name: Input and output resources
values.variables.0.change: Conceptually review reading and writing the same array
values.variables.0.expected: The same-array approach is expected to have possible order dependence and will not be used as the reference.
values.criteria.0: The maximum error over three steps is within the chosen 1e-5 tolerance.
values.criteria.1: Record each step's read and write buffer ids.
values.questions.0: Can independent-element updates write in place?
values.questions.1: Does workgroupBarrier guarantee the previous state of another workgroup?

values.title: Mapping and Staging Buffers
values.concepts.0.title: Readback Path
values.concepts.0.explanation: Reading a GPU storage buffer directly on the CPU differs from the usual readback contract. Copy to a COPY_DST|MAP_READ staging buffer, then map it.
values.concepts.1.title: Mapped State
values.concepts.1.explanation: A mapped buffer cannot be used by the GPU. Copy the getMappedRange data for retention before calling unmap.
values.steps.0: In readback.js, separate the result COPY_SRC buffer from the staging buffer.
values.steps.1: Submit copyBufferToBuffer, then await mapAsync(GPUMapMode.READ).
values.steps.2: Copy getMappedRange data, unmap, and then perform the next calculation.
values.variables.0.name: Read count
values.variables.0.expected: Repeated mapping and waiting are expected to increase end-to-end latency.
values.criteria.0: Copied CPU results remain available after unmap.
values.criteria.1: Do not reuse a mapped staging buffer in GPU commands.
values.questions.0: What changes after unmap if you retain the getMappedRange view directly?
values.questions.1: Is readback necessary when you only display GPU results?

values.title: Copy Alignment and Texture Rows
values.concepts.0.title: Buffer Copies
values.concepts.0.explanation: copyBufferToBuffer offsets and sizes require 4-byte alignment. Record total buffer capacity separately from the valid data length.
values.concepts.1.title: Texture Rows
values.concepts.1.explanation: For encoder buffer↔texture copies, use a bytesPerRow multiple of 256 bytes where required. Do not confuse this with queue.writeTexture row rules.
values.steps.0: In copy-layout.js, for a 13-pixel RGBA8 row, calculate the 52 valid bytes and padded stride 256.
values.steps.1: Reconstruct the CPU image by skipping padding in the copyTextureToBuffer result.
values.steps.2: Compare buffer copy offset 4 and invalid offset 2 with an error scope.
values.variables.0.name: Row stride
values.variables.0.expected: Excluding padding is expected to restore the original 13-pixel row.
values.criteria.0: Record valid row bytes and copy stride separately.
values.criteria.1: The reconstructed image matches the original, and the invalid offset produces a validation error.
values.questions.0: Must the multiple-of-256 rule always apply to writeTexture too?
values.questions.1: What stripes appear if padding is read as pixels?
values.prerequisites: Continue using the output and notes from unit 17. Preserve the previous inputs and reference outputs before the Copy Alignment and Texture Rows experiment.

values.title: Workgroup Shared Memory
values.concepts.0.title: Sharing Scope
values.concepts.0.explanation: var<workgroup> is shared by invocations in the same workgroup. Different workgroups cannot communicate through this memory.
values.concepts.1.title: Synchronization
values.concepts.1.explanation: Use workgroupBarrier to synchronize writes at that stage before reading shared values. The entire workgroup must reach the barrier in uniform control flow.
values.steps.0: In reduce.wgsl, write a partial-sum kernel that places 64 values in a workgroup array.
values.steps.1: Have out-of-range lanes write 0 and participate in the barrier too.
values.steps.2: For N=65, sum the two partial sums on the CPU and compare with the full sum.
values.variables.0.name: Length
values.variables.0.expected: Empty lanes in the second group are expected to participate with 0, producing the correct sum.
values.criteria.0: The CPU sum of 65 elements and the sum of GPU partial sums agree within tolerance.
values.criteria.1: There is no path where only some lanes return before the barrier.
values.questions.0: Does a barrier synchronize the entire dispatch?
values.questions.1: Why fill out-of-range lanes with 0?
values.prerequisites: Continue using the output and notes from unit 18. Preserve the previous inputs and reference outputs before the Workgroup Shared Memory experiment.

values.title: Rendering Compute Results
values.concepts.0.title: Connections Within the GPU
values.concepts.0.explanation: Compute results can be rendered directly as vertex or storage input. A later pass in the same submission can consume results without CPU readback.
values.concepts.1.title: Usage Declarations
values.concepts.1.explanation: Declare the usages needed for both compute writes and render reads on the buffer. State roles between passes to avoid conflicts.
values.steps.0: In particles.js, create a position STORAGE|VERTEX|COPY_SRC|COPY_DST buffer and a velocity STORAGE|COPY_DST buffer, and write initial data with writeBuffer.
values.steps.1: Update positions in the compute pass, then use them as vertex positions in the following render pass.
values.steps.2: Connect readback only to a validation button and display calls per frame.
values.variables.0.name: Readback policy
values.variables.0.expected: The visual result is expected to remain unchanged, while CPU waiting cost may decrease.
values.criteria.0: Ordinary frames make 0 mapAsync calls.
values.criteria.1: The validation button's position values agree with the CPU reference within tolerance.
values.questions.0: Why does overlapping reads and writes within one pass need review?
values.questions.1: Does adding a usage automatically copy data?
values.prerequisites: Continue using the output and notes from unit 19. Preserve the previous inputs and reference outputs before the Rendering Compute Results experiment.

values.title: Instancing and Data Structures
values.concepts.0.title: Instances
values.concepts.0.explanation: When drawing the same base shape repeatedly, instance indices can retrieve individual data. Draw-call count and screen fragment count are different costs.
values.concepts.1.title: Array Structure
values.concepts.1.explanation: AoS and SoA differ in management and access patterns depending on data access. Measure structural benefits in the actual kernel.
values.outcomes.1: Distinguish call count from processing volume.
values.steps.0: In instance.wgsl, read position and color storage arrays using instance_index.
values.steps.1: Draw a small quad as 256 instances in one draw.
values.steps.2: Record draw counts and frame intervals for 64·256·512 particles.
values.variables.0.name: Instance count
values.variables.0.expected: The draw count is expected to stay the same while vertex and fragment processing increases.
values.criteria.0: There is one draw call at all three counts.
values.criteria.1: Check four markers to confirm each instance reads its own position and color.
values.questions.0: Does one draw call imply constant rendering cost?
values.questions.1: Which is always faster, AoS or SoA?
values.prerequisites: Continue using the output and notes from unit 20. Preserve the previous inputs and reference outputs before the Instancing and Data Structures experiment.

values.title: Device Loss and Reinitialization
values.concepts.0.title: Lost State
values.concepts.0.explanation: device.lost signals that the device is no longer valid. Resources from the previous device cannot be reused unchanged on a new device.
values.concepts.1.title: Recreation
values.concepts.1.explanation: Recovery needs a path that recreates shaders, buffers, and pipelines. Retain CPU settings and initial data in a reproducible form.
values.steps.0: In device.js, connect device.lost handling to stopping the render loop.
values.steps.1: Call device.destroy from a development button and display the loss reason.
values.steps.2: On explicit user retry, create a new device and resources and restore saved settings.
values.variables.0.name: Device state
values.variables.0.expected: The loop is expected to stop and recover with new resources after an explicit retry.
values.criteria.0: Do not submit to the previous device after loss.
values.criteria.1: After retry, create the same initial scene with a new device.
values.questions.0: Should retry policies for a destroy reason and unexpected loss be identical?
values.questions.1: What information must remain on the CPU for recovery?
values.prerequisites: Continue using the output and notes from unit 21. Preserve the previous inputs and reference outputs before the Device Loss and Reinitialization experiment.

values.title: Asynchronous Errors and Task Identity
values.concepts.0.title: Error Channels
values.concepts.0.explanation: Error scopes and uncapturederror are different error observation paths. Display expected validation failures separately from unexpected errors.
values.concepts.1.title: Generation Numbers
values.concepts.1.explanation: Earlier asynchronous work can finish during reinitialization. Use a device generation number to prevent stale results from modifying new state.
values.outcomes.1: Block stale results from being applied.
values.steps.0: In errors.js, add an uncapturederror listener and task labels.
values.steps.1: Create a delayed fixture that requests reinitialization during pipeline creation.
values.steps.2: Compare the completed result's generation and record discarded earlier results.
values.variables.0.name: Completion order
values.variables.0.expected: The late result is expected not to replace the new pipeline.
values.criteria.0: Error logs display the task label and generation.
values.criteria.1: Only current-generation resources are used in both completion orders.
values.questions.0: Why does an overly broad error scope make tracing causes harder?
values.questions.1: What cleanup is needed when discarding a stale pipeline result?
values.prerequisites: Continue using the output and notes from unit 22. Preserve the previous inputs and reference outputs before the Asynchronous Errors and Task Identity experiment.

values.title: The Scope of Timing
values.concepts.0.title: End-to-End Latency
values.concepts.0.explanation: The interval from the CPU-side start to completed readback includes transfer and waiting. Do not interpret it as compute kernel execution time.
values.concepts.1.title: Optional Measurement
values.concepts.1.explanation: Use timestamp-query only after checking support and requesting it. If unsupported, leave the GPU interval unmeasured and provide CPU elapsed time.
values.steps.0: In benchmark.js, separate input generation, upload, submission, and map-completion intervals.
values.steps.1: Record timestamp-query support and configure pass timestamps and the resolve path only when supported.
values.steps.2: After warmup, save end-to-end latencies for five runs and any available GPU interval values in separate columns.
values.variables.0.name: Array size
values.variables.0.expected: Computation is expected to increase, while fixed transfer costs are more prominent for small inputs.
values.criteria.0: Record end-to-end latency and GPU intervals under different names.
values.criteria.1: Do not request unsupported features, and state which items remain unmeasured.
values.questions.0: Is elapsed onSubmittedWorkDone time kernel time?
values.questions.1: Why might the first run before warmup be slow?
values.prerequisites: Continue using the output and notes from unit 23. Preserve the previous inputs and reference outputs before starting "The Scope of Timing".

values.title: CPU References and Error Budgets
values.concepts.0.title: Floating Point
values.concepts.0.explanation: CPU JavaScript number and GPU f32 operations have different precision. Summation with a different association order can produce small errors.
values.concepts.1.title: Validation Criteria
values.concepts.1.explanation: Absolute and relative error serve different roles depending on magnitude. Define tolerances and special-value handling before viewing results.
values.steps.0: In reference.js, write a CPU particle-update function and generate fixed-seed inputs.
values.steps.1: Calculate per-element absolute and relative errors against the readback result.
values.steps.2: For inputs containing 0, negative, small, and large values, print the maximum error and failing indices.
values.variables.0.name: Validation input
values.variables.0.change: Mix of 0, negative, and large values
values.variables.0.expected: Inputs of different magnitudes are expected to expose limitations of a relative-error-only criterion.
values.criteria.0: Record the tolerance abs<=1e-5+1e-4*abs(reference) in advance.
values.criteria.1: On failure, print the element index, reference value, and GPU value.
values.questions.0: Which tasks require exactly identical bit results?
values.questions.1: Can including NaN in error comparisons allow a check to pass?
values.prerequisites: Continue using the output and notes from unit 24. Preserve the previous inputs and reference outputs before the CPU References and Error Budgets experiment.

values.title: Workgroup Size Experiments
values.concepts.0.title: Configuration Constraints
values.concepts.0.explanation: Workgroup size must satisfy both device limits and the shader declaration. Larger sizes are not always faster.
values.concepts.1.title: Fair Comparison
values.concepts.1.explanation: Compare identical inputs, operations, and readback policies. Changing the algorithm along with kernel configuration makes causes hard to isolate.
values.steps.0: In tuning.js, prepare 32·64·128-lane kernel variants and check limits.
values.steps.1: Run the same N=1003 input with each configuration.
values.steps.2: After checking correctness, save five end-to-end latency runs and the list of supported configurations.
values.variables.0.name: Workgroup size
values.variables.0.expected: Execution efficiency is expected to depend on the device, while all configurations should produce the same results.
values.criteria.0: All three configurations pass the CPU reference through the last element.
values.criteria.1: Skip unsupported configurations and record why.
values.questions.0: How does a larger workgroup affect shared-memory use?
values.questions.1: Is it appropriate to fix one device's optimum as the default?
values.prerequisites: Continue using the output and notes from unit 25. Preserve the previous inputs and reference outputs before starting "Workgroup Size Experiments".

values.title: Acceptance of the Integrated Particle Experiment
values.concepts.0.title: Separate Components
values.concepts.0.explanation: Separating initial data, kernels, rendering, readback, and UI clarifies error locations. Module contracts include buffer sizes and lifetimes.
values.concepts.1.title: Acceptance Evidence
values.concepts.1.explanation: Visible animation alone cannot prove computational correctness. Keep failure-recovery and CPU-comparison results together.
values.outcomes.1: Perform acceptance checks including failures and restarts.
values.steps.0: In README.md, tabulate each module's inputs, outputs, and resource ownership.
values.steps.1: Run five scenarios: unsupported environment, device loss, resize, N=0, and N=1003.
values.steps.2: Export the current settings JSON and CPU-comparison results, then restore them in a new session.
values.variables.0.name: Starting state
values.variables.0.expected: The same initial data is expected to be reproduced without hidden GPU state.
values.criteria.0: Each of the five scenarios has an actual observation or a reason it was not run.
values.criteria.1: The seed and initial positions match after restart.
values.questions.0: What computational errors can remain hidden in apparently normal animation?
values.questions.1: Which GPU work need not be created for empty input?
